subtopic: PAKISTAN TO BECOME INDEPENDENT REPUBLIC WITHIN COMMONWEALTH

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PAKISTAN TO BECOME INDEPENDENT REPUBLIC WITHIN COMMONWEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to inform the house of a declaration issued from the prime ministers' conference at two p.m. eastern standard time today, as follows:
The government of Pakistan have informed the other governments of the commonwealth of the intention of the Pakistan people that, under the new constitution which is about to be adopted, Pakistan shall become a sovereign, independent republic. The government of Pakistan have, however, declared and affirmed Pakistan's desire to continue her full membership of the commonwealth of nations and her acceptance of the Queen as the symbol of the free association of its independent member nations, and as such the head of the commonwealth. The governments of the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Ceylon, the basis of whose membership is not hereby changed, accept and recognize Pakistan's continuing membership in accordance with the terms of this declaration. The government of India, the basis of whose membership is also unaltered, similarly recognize Pakistan's continuing membership.
In notifying the other prime ministers of Pakistan's intention, Mr. Mohammed Ali reaffirmed his country's steadfast adherence to the commonwealth. The other prime ministers, in accepting this proposal, welcomed Pakistan's continued association and co-operation as a member of the commonwealth and assured Mr. Mohammed Ali that the friendship and good will of their countries towards Pakistan would remain unaffected by this constitutional change.
Accordingly, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Pakistan and Ceylon hereby declare, as they did in 1949 when a similar decision was taken in respect of India, that they remain united as free and equal members of the commonwealth of nations, freely co-operating in the pursuit of peace, liberty and progress.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, all hon. members and all Canadians will rejoice in this new demonstration of the traditional capacity of the commonwealth to strengthen its unity of purpose while adapting its organization and procedures to changed circumstances. Everyone will rejoice in the fact that, notwithstanding the exercise by the people of Pakistan of their right to determine the form of their domestic government, it has been found possible to have Pakistan remain a member of the commonwealth and to continue for the peace of the world the association of those nations whose traditions give
them the same concept of a proper way of living and of democratic processes designed to further the welfare of the men and women of their respective nations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Is the minister aware that a considerable number of former owners of property in the Gagetown camp area have not agreed to settlement of their claims and consequently have not received payment for property taken over by the department, nor have arbitration proceedings or legal action been started? In consideration of the serious financial position in which these people are

Inquiries of the Ministry placed as a result, will the department arrange for part payment of these claims pending future settlement?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: GAGETOWN CAMP
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question. I find that out of 1,630 claims involved in the Gagetown expropriation, over 92 per cent have been settled amicably, and without resort to litigation-which I think constitutes a very excellent record on the part of the departmental officers.
Of the claims where settlement is still uncompleted, some are delayed because the owners or heirs cannot be found, or because the owners or heirs of estates cannot agree as to their own idea of price, or for various other technical reasons.
I might say that expropriation proceedings are about to be initiated in a few cases. Cash advances have been made on a number of occasions to persons whose property has not yet been settled for, where need has been demonstrated, I was of the view that all such cases had been taken care of, but if the hon. member knows of any persons who are suffering hardship among the few that are left, and will give me their names, I shall be pleased to have such cases looked into.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself caught in a rather odd geographical position just now between conflicting forces. The last thing I want to do is to get into any internecine warfare between the various branches of the Conservative party. That is entirely their business and none of mine. But I do admire the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) when he gets up and says that he is going to cast politics aside and then for 40 minutes simply refuses to take his own advice. Possibly he was just as wise, as I do not know how anyone in this house can cast politics aside.
But I shall take your advice, Mr. Speaker, and deal with national matters in a rather different sense. I am not concerned with warfare on this side. As far as I am concerned the enemy is in the other part of the house where I can see the whites of their eyes. I feel sufficiently inimical today to ask certain questions, especially of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), because the government owes these answers to parliament and


to the country. They are matters of common concern about which all of us are perturbed. We do not know what the facts are and we have no inkling yet of what government policy will be. We should like to know what the answers are.
In the first place it is time we knew exactly the status of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and the position of the government with regard to that company. Is it the government's intention to subsidize private enterprise, or is it the government's intention to insist that private enterprise stand on its own feet? Is the treasury of the people of Canada to be looted once again in order to help private enterprise, or is it not? These are questions which I should like to have answered.
It is of course a piece of outstanding impertinence for any believer in private enterprise to suggest means whereby the treasury of the people of Canada is used to support private enterprise. The government will have to make up its mind whether it is going to help this pipe-line company or whether it is going to take over this pipe line as we in the C.C.F. have advocated. If a subsidy is granted, if a guarantee is granted, if the government is going to take the risk then the government should take the profits.
We have long said that the national interest demands that this pipe line be owned by the people of this country. We say so for two reasons. The first and obvious one is that we want to protect the consumer. I am quite certain that were this pipe line nationally owned gas would be provided to the consumer at from 30 per cent to 40 per cent below what it will be by a commercial corporation.
Then we also have to protect the future. I fear that if this pipe line comes under private enterprise it will be pushed through by men without the vision or imagination to realize what Canada will be like ten or fifteen years hence. The pipe line will be completely inadequate for the needs of this country. We shall have a 30-inch pipe line in the next year or two perhaps, and in ten years we may require another 30-inch pipe line. That is surely a squandering of capital if ever I saw it. If the job is going to be done, let it be done properly now. If this company does not have the finances to do the job properly, let the government take it on as a matter of service to the people of Canada. As I said, to do otherwise would be to waste money.
Yet here we have private enterprise once again coming to the treasury of the people of Canada asking for a subsidy, asking for a handout. None of us knows what the cost

will be. It might be nothing; it might be $15 million; it might be many millions more. None of us at the present time know. All we do know is that the treasury of Canada is being asked to guarantee the profits of Texas tycoons who will do their very best during the coming years to take as much as they can out of the pockets of the people of Canada.
Maybe some will say that if this guarantee does not go through it will be against the national interest, that the pipe line ought to be started this year. If it is so much in the national interest, let the government do the job and let us not .subsidize foreigners. We have done that in the past to our cost.
As for the capitalization of the company, we still do not know what it is going to be. I have heard it said that there will be $50 million share capital out of an investment of $300 million, the rest of course being in the form of bonds. Forecasts have been made as to the possible financial position of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited within a few years. I saw one in the Financial Post that within five years this company would be showing a profit, after depreciation, after the payment of bond interest and before taxes, of $20 million a year. A return of $20 million a year on an investment capital outlay of $50 million or $60 million is a pretty handsome return. That is the sort of return which this group whom I call Texas tycoons are going after.
The best thing that could happen would be for the government to take over the whole proposition and do the job. This in other fields has been done already by one minister of the government whose political philosophy was born yesterday and will die tomorrow. I refer to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who nevertheless has done a first-class job with Trans-Canada Air Lines and Polymer Corporation. I only hope that he has the wisdom to see the necessity of the people of Canada owning this pipe line. We in the C.C.F. will never for one moment consent to its being subsidized by the treasury of Canada.
There is another matter in our minds which is perhaps of greater general interest. I refer to the whole question of foreign investment in Canada. Most of the foreign investment here is American, although quite a substantial part is European. And under certain conditions I welcome both. I welcome more European investment because I want to see greater diversity of investment in this country, rather than have us almost in thraldom to one country.
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
But the significant thing is that when one looks at the financial structure of Canada one is struck by the small, the almost insignificant part which Canadian capital itself has played in the opening up of this country. When I think of the Canadian capitalist 1 think about what Robert Burns said about the mouse- the "tim'rous beastie". Unquestionably, when it comes to investment in their own country, Canadian capitalists are frightened, cowardly creatures depending always upon outsiders to do the job which they should be doing themselves. They are men without vision, men without confidence, men without any courage whatsoever. I think of what the future of Canada has for all of us, and then I realize that Canadian capitalism has abdicated in favour of the foreigners. And that is a dangerous situation.

speechtext:
I cannot help that. But my point is this, in this particular context, that we have been depending upon foreign capital coming into Canada to develop this country, and to open it up.
One can have only admiration for the drive and energy the Americans have shown in exploring and developing this country. But my regard for them, my admiration for that drive and energy ceases when it appears that American capital is going to own Canada. We are getting into the position where, very definitely, in the economic sense we are becoming an American satellite. Where you have economic strength, there you have political strength; where you have economic ownership, there you ultimately have political ownership. And I object to Canada's being regarded as either an economic or a political annex of the United States.
I condemn the pattern; I oppose the trend; and my fear at the moment is that the government, by its inaction in this matter, is selling Canada into economic bondage. And all that we can do to oppose it will be done.
There are three kinds of investment in the country just now. There is that which is known as the sticks and stones investment- investment in buildings, investment in plants, investment in machinery, investment in these means of production by which employment is given and Canadian wealth is increased. That is good investment. That is the sort of investment that we-and quite rightly-ought to encourage, although I would like to see Canadians doing much more of it. I would like to see Canadians taking the risks which some of the Americans have been taking. And obviously, if Canadians themselves are not going to do it, then others are going to do it.
But this also has been very obvious during the last year. There has been a very definite switch in investments, which is now taking two other forms; and in a highly vulnerable economy such as ours they are dangerous.
(Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).]

In this connection I shall quote a paragraph from the monthly review issued by the Bank of Nova Scotia, where it says:
Moreover, the apparent dependence of the current premium on capital movements not directly associated with Canadian economic growth is scarcely reassuring. So long as the bulk of the capital inflow took the form of direct investment by United States firms and direct borrowing in New York by Canadian provinces and municipalities, the inflow was actually financing the development of resources and industry and was predominantly of a long-term nature. Over the past year, however, there has been some slackening in the pace of Canadian development, and at the same time a sudden increase in the inflow of funds for investment in existing securities.
It is this sudden .inflow of funds which ought to be causing more alarm than apparently it is at the moment on the treasury benches. There is this great investment in Canadian companies, which will last just as long as the profit situation lasts. For money, in itself, knows no patriotism; money follows no flag; money only follows profits. And such investment can be very dangerous to the economy of one's country.
When we look at the Canadian scene we can see what is happening. There is the type of investment coming into this country which is buying stocks and shares for long-term investment, and buying them in such magnitude that Canadian industry is being taken over by the United States. One can think of oil, of foodstuffs, of automobiles, of the electrical industry; and there are others. And what must be the disturbing feature to the Canadian investor is this, that there are stocks and shares of Canadian corporations being bought at prices greater than a projection of company earnings justifies. And that, in itself, can be dangerous for Canadians, although it implies a faith in Canada which I think is well justified.
However, as I said earlier, where you have this economic control in a country, eventually you will get political domination. And again Canada may be in the position of being grateful to Quebec for once more saving this nation, as such.
There is a third type of investment, and this is really a dangerous type which we see before us today. I refer to investment by non-resident-owned investment corporations. They are posing a very serious threat to the Canadian economy.
First of all I think we ought to consider what is happening in the American market just now. It could be said fairly I think that in the American stock market we see people who are the victims of Coueism-who believe that they are going to be better off and better off every day in every way. They apparently believe in a chicken in every pot and a car in

every garage and a portfolio of investments in every safe. And they are not going to achieve their ambitions.
Perhaps this optimism is prompted by a statement made by the President of the United States last October, before the election, when he said that national production in the United States might reach $500 billion in ten years' time. Others have said the same thing during the last few months, although there are very responsible economists in the United States who take grave issue with this, and who warn the people in that country of the dangers which are almost obvious in their own economic situation.
One of the most alarming is the gap between stock prices and production indices. Unless that gap is met, is narrowed, there will be trouble. Perhaps one could call the present situation by a name other than Coueism; perhaps we should call it voodoo prosperity, prosperity by incantation. But the power of that voodooism extends now to Canada and is threatening our own investment.
The exchange situation between Canada and the United States is about as unhealthy as it could possibly be. The exchange rate in no way whatsoever reflects the balance of trade between the two nations. The exchange rate is something spurious and synthetic and ultimately dangerous to the Canadian economy.
Then within the last few months we have had this greatest danger of all, namely financial investment or finance investment- let me put it that way-which has been so greatly responsible for the rise of the Canadian dollar. For instance, in June of last year the United States dollar was at a discount of 1-7/8 points. In July it was at a discount of 2-9/16 points. Yet in those two months the Canadian government, through the exchange fund, bought $71 million of United States funds in an attempt to stop our dollar rising and they were completely and totally unsuccessful. The situation has become worse despite the fact that the exchange equalization fund has been buying United States dollars. It became so much worse in August that, despite the attempt of the Bank of Canada, the discount on the U.S. dollar went to 3 per cent and in December it rose to 3-7/32. That is an extremely serious thing for Canada in more ways than one.
I am not going to go into the implications to Canada from the point of view of exports or from the point of view of imports. At the moment I am dealing with the matter solely in the restricted sphere of finance. We have these non-resident investment corporations which, in the last few months, I am convinced, have poured $150 million into this
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart country and probably more; I think $150 million would be a conservative estimate. This inflow of money does not assist in any way the development of this country. In fact it will become a definite hindrance. These shares are sold only to United States investors. It is true that in Canada there is a 15 per cent withholding tax on the dividends of these corporations, on the money received; but then there are no dividends declared by those corporations because the Americans are in them for capital gain. They do not want to see any dividends declared. All income which comes in is used to buy still more Canadian securities on the market.
One of the reasons for this desire for capital gain is, of course, that Americans feel that they will be better off in the long run by paying a lesser capital gains tax than a larger income tax. They have funds which are known as open-end funds. There is no limit to them. As long as there is demand in the United States, these United States funds will be used to buy Canadian securities in unlimited quantities. Of course, if they can buy them, they can also sell them. That is one of the things which should perhaps give us pause because if, perchance, it should so happen that there were a break in confidence, one can imagine the sort of break which would occur on the stock markets of this country and one can well imagine how many Canadian investors would be wiped out.
The main problem is this: What is being done about it? The government may say, "We are using the exchange equalization fund". I do not think they are doing so to any substantial extent but I am not prepared to blame them for that. The exchange equalization fund has in the past shown itself to be inadequate and it is an extremely expensive way of working. I remember that in 1950 there was a determined move on the part of United States capital to come to this country. The exchange equalization fund spent $600 million in buying United States currency in order to try to stop that movement but they could not hope to dam the flood. That was a heavy outlay of money. I do not think for a moment that the exchange fund can have any great effect on the situation as it exists, although it should still be used.
One other reason for United States money coming into this country is the attraction of a long-term interest rate somewhat higher than that which exists in the United States. The obvious way to cure that situation is by means of open market operations by the Bank of Canada whereby our interest rate is brought down to such a level that it offers no attraction to the Americans and, as far

The Address-Mr. Patterson as Canadians are concerned, is an inducement to Canadians, if they are going to go into long-term borrowing, to do their borrowing on the Canadian market rather than on the United States market.
The exchange equalization fund must be used. Bank of Canada policy must be such that the interest rate is kept below that of the United States as far as possible. But neither of these two suggestions gets us away from the problem of what to do about these non-resident investment corporations which are creating so much havoc. I think there is only one answer. I should like to hear what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has to say because he must provide an answer. He must give an answer to Canada as to what government policy is going to be in this matter. I think the only answer is to impose on these corporations punitive, frankly discriminatory taxes which will discourage them from coming into Canada and operating in the way in which they operate. They are operating quite properly from their point of view or from anybody's point of view, but the net effect of their operations is to create an extremely serious economic problem within Canada. That problem must be faced and an answer must be found for it. I do not think at the moment there is any answer other than a punitive tax on these corporations; a tax on their income even although it is not distributed; a tax heavy enough to dissuade any others from coming into this market.
There are plans afoot whereby tens of millions of United States dollars are going to come into this country in the near future in the form of non-resident investment corporations and they are merely going to make our exchange situation so much worse. I maintain that the most serious problem today in finance which the minister has to solve is this one with respect to these corporations. He must find an answer. He must give an answer to this house so that we shall know what we are doing. If no answer is given and if this unhealthy situation continues between the Canadian and the American dollars, then, as I said earlier, it will be proof that the government is prepared to sell Canada into economic bondage.

Mr. Speaker, now that we have arrived at the point when the main motion is to be discussed, there are a number of matters which I wish to bring up. We have been debating this motion since January 10, following the speeches made by the mover and the seconder on January 7, with the exception of four days or so during which we discussed matters of international importance.
In the years I have been in this house, having regard to the problems that face our country, I have never seen a ministry so silent in respect of those things about which the people of Canada are seeking information. What is to be done for the unemployed? With the exception of a qualified promise in the speech from the throne and a temporary expedient in the form of legislation already passed by parliament, there is no suggestion of what is to be done. There is nothing in regard to trade and the loss of markets abroad. A total of 55 or 56 supporters of the government have spoken, but not one minister has given answers to the major problems facing Canada; not a word regarding our loss of trade. Day after day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has sat and listened, but not a word from him. Nothing in regard to what took place at the conference in Washington; nothing in regard to the measures to be taken to secure trade in various parts of the world. Parliament has been treated in recent weeks by the cabinet with a cavalier disregard of the rights of the Canadian people, and almost with condescension.
The House of Commons is becoming nothing but a tape recorder for the cabinet, a constitutional nuisance to be tolerated by the cabinet. Some announcements are made outside the house while parliament is sitting, such as the announcement regarding the granting of a licence to Canadian Pacific Air Lines to operate a trans-polar route or the
announcement yesterday by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) regarding a matter that affects agriculture, not only in British Columbia but in Ontario and Quebec. I refer to the reduction in the subsidies on feed grains.	.
We ask questions, returns are passed, months go by. On several occasions recently hon. members of this house have tried to find out about Canadian National employees who stand in jeopardy of losing their positions, many in fact already having lost them. On January 26 I endeavoured to bring up this matter in the form of a question. I inquired about lay-offs of employees of the Canadian National Railways. These employees want to know what is the policy. They hear that on the western division some $3,500,000 is to be saved by the simple expedient of cutting off the heads of the lower employees, the labouring men, rather than giving consideration to reducing some of the extremely high salaries of officials at the top.
We are told nothing in regard to trade. There is no adequate answer by any minister of the crown regarding the position of agriculture in this country; no answer by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to what is to be done about the situation revealed by the dominion bureau of statistics, which shows that trade is decreasing. We have tried to get information from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I understand that he has a speech on the subject of trade in cold storage; let him bring it out. On January 10, as reported on pages 19 and 20 of Hansard, I asked the following question to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is he in a position to say anything regarding the visit of three ministers of the government to Washington recently, and whether or not the United States government has given any indication that it intends to discontinue its apparent policy of applying quotas and embargoes against Canadian agricultural products?

Before the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is completed I hope to make a statement on Canadian trade policy which I think will contain the information my hon. friend is seeking. The visit to the United States concerned a number of matters. It would be difficult to answer the hon. member's question categorically, but I think the information will be forthcoming in the next two or three weeks.
On February 1 the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) directed some questions to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with GATT, to which the minister replied as follows:
Owing to the length of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, it seemed to me that I could contribute more to the expedition of the business of the house if I refrained from speaking. I have heard no great interest in trade matters displayed in this

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
debate, and perhaps in the circumstances the statement could be deferred until an appropriate bill is before the house or until later in the session.
Such diffidence, such consideration for the sensibilities of parliament, has not in the past been one of the characteristics of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. According to a report in the Canadian press dated January 7, when the minister returned from Washington he said:
Trade Minister Howe, on return from his Washington trip last night, said it may take a "few days" to find out what results his talks with United States cabinet ministers had.
Some "compromises" are likely, he said in an interview, but at the moment he could not say what impact they will have on international negotiations to strengthen the seven-year trade pact.
He said he would know in a few days. When I asked a question on January 10 he gave the house to understand that before this debate concluded he would speak to the house on this matter which affects the Canadian people more than any other problem. We have not had a word. Are we coming to the end of GATT? Are we in such a position that the minister cannot make one of his periodical optimistic statements?
Surely parliament has a right to know what is taking place. I note that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who could not answer certain questions asked in parliament last week, found it necessary to wait until he left for the old country before parliament was told what it could not find out when he was here. Are we to have to wait until the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in Australia or New Zealand several weeks hence before we are to find out about this policy? We ask the minister to bring out that speech which is in cold storage and let the people know what he has done, what took place at Washington and what he expects will be the situation in the days that lie ahead.
What of our trade? The optimism which was displayed by the minister in January and February of 1954 has been dissipated in the light of our experience since then. I am not going into many statistics; I am simply going to point out that the preliminary figures for the full year 1954 are now available, and that our total exports in 1954 amounted to $3,942 million whereas in the previous year they amounted to $4,173 million. So far as imports are concerned they too have been reduced during the year by approximately $280 million.
The total trade for 1954 including exports and imports was $8,037 million, while in 1953 it was $8,556 million. What is going to be done? Has GATT collapsed? Recent reports in

the Financial Post give some indication of what took place. And I am not going to restrict the request for a report to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) could tell us whether the United States administration has a policy all its own, and whether it refused to consider objections raised or the alternatives offered on the part of Canadian representatives when they were in Washington. Why this silence? Over the years we used to get these reports regularly during the session, but for some reason or other in 1955 the optimistic reports of the past are unavailable.
The minister dare not speak and tell what actually took place in 1954. As a matter of fact one of the government's former officials, Gerald Godsoe, who during the period of the war occupied a high position in the government of this country, said while speaking before the Chautauqua Institution in July of last year:
One of our problems is the decided risk we run in having so many of our eggs, and such large ones, in the same basket-in our present dependency on your market. This makes it ever-important for us that ... we concentrate diligently on greatly improving our trade with Britain.
Then he went on to say:
The United States for a long time to come will be dependent on Canada for certain minerals and other natural resources and products. From the point of view of the Canadian economy it is desirable to have a larger proportion of these taken in the future in manufactures rather than in the raw or simply processed form.
Thereby he gives support to the policy of this party so often enunciated, and repeated so recently by the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe).
During the period between January and November what happened to our farm income? What happened to our farm markets? Some days ago the minister indicated that there was nothing to worry about. There has been some increase in wheat marketing since November, but the wheat record for 1954 is a sorry commentary on the policies of this government. Here is the record, according to the bulletin issued January 13 by the dominion bureau of statistics. Excerpts from that report indicate that domestic exports of all products to the United States in the 11-month period declined to $2,097,-
705,000	from $2,199,713,000. Exports of all products to the United Kingdom in the same period of 1954 went down from $617,908,000 to $575,583,000. So far as commonwealth countries are concerned, the report says that in the 11-month period exports to all other commonwealth countries declined to $178,-
702,000	from $219,402,000, or by approximately $41 million. For the Latin-American countries, in the same 11 months as compared

with the 11 months in 1953, trade dropped from $183,242,000 to $168,009,000. Everywhere in the world our markets are disappearing.
The ministers travel. They make peregrinations and pilgrimages here, there and everywhere. I cannot use "pilgrimate" as a verb, but I think it could be said that while they "pilgrimate" trade stagnates.
What about wheat? Well, the record cannot be laughed off any longer. On a number of occasions in 1954 the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) indicated in this house that we were losing our markets for wheat. The answer was that there was nothing to worry about but that wheat marketings were keeping up. So far as wheat is concerned, exports between January and November of 1953 amounted to $530,903,000, while during the same period in 1954 those exports were valued at $339,871,000, or a decrease of $190,000,000.
Surely those are not figures that support the optimistic attitude displayed by this government. I think they indicate and display the reason for the unaccustomed silence on trade matters by the ministers of this government, who in the past have boasted about increases in trade throughout the years. What about wheat flour? Exports of wheat flour between January and November 1954 were valued at $81,371,000, while in the same period of 1953 they were valued at $93,590,000, or a fall of approximately $12 million.
What about other grains, that is grains other than wheat? The record is even worse, proportionately. Between January and November, 1953, exports of other grains amounted to $196,263,000, while during the corresponding period of 1954 they were $115,915,000, or a fall of approximately $81 million.
Those records tell the story. They indict this government for its failure to look after trade, for its failure to act, and for its continued reliance upon optimistic statements rather than actual statistics. As to shipments of wheat the record is lamentable. I am not going to quote it unless someone wishes me to do so, but an article appearing early in February by the Canadian Press indicates that all major grain countries except Canada showed increased wheat exports in the first four months of the current crop year. Canada's shipments dropped in those four months by
6.100.000	bushels, the bureau of statistics reported. United States exports in the same period increased to 72,500,000 bushels from 70,000,000 bushels; Argentine exports increased by approximately 2,000,000 bushels to
45.200.000	bushels; Australia's exports increased by approximately 4,700,000 bushels to
26.700.000	bushels.

It is all very well to say that shipments are falling behind demand and sales. The record indicates that we have lost in considerable degree not only our markets for wheat but also our competitive possibilities as against the other wheat producers. That is the picture, Mr. Speaker, upon which the Canadian people ask for information-encouragement, if you will-from the government, rather than the silence that has characterized this government in recent days.

I again ask the minister and the government to let the house and the country know the situation with regard to the trade position, and also the measures that are to be taken to meet this serious situation resulting from extraordinarily strong competition by other countries, and also resulting from the high price tags placed on Canadian products by reason, in considerable measure, of the unnecessarily high taxes which are imposed by this government and which have continued in existence for several years.
For almost a month, Mr. Speaker, with the exception of the interlude of four days during which we discussed the international situation, parliament has been endeavouring to secure information, first, on the matter of unemployment and what is being done to meet it. That is something that affects every part of our country and every industry and every group of people within this country. I ask that information be given with regard to the railway employees who, because of the fact that they work for a government corporation, have not that freedom to speak which those who work for other than government corporations enjoy and have the right to expect.
Then we want to know what is being done with regard to the question of farm markets. A few days ago the matter of the importation of cheese was raised and the Minister of Trade and Commerce glibly said we had nothing to do with that, that the import permit legislation did not apply in the case of cheese being dumped into this country. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Hast-ings-Frontenac (Mr. White) showed conclusively that under the orders in council in effect under the Agricultural Prices Support Act power is conferred upon the government, whenever floor prices in our country are being interfered with in any way or when the floor policy is being in any way undermined, to utilize the authority contained in that act. Yet a few days ago, when asked in effect, "What are you going to do about it?" the minister said, in effect "There is nothing we can do. Anyway, they promised us that there would not be any more for a period of several months."
Surely, Mr. Speaker, having regard to agricultural conditions today, the falling income

of farmers throughout this country, the rise in the cost of the things the farmer has to buy, the farmer has a right to expect such action as the laws of the country permit to the end that agricultural prosperity shall not be unnecessarily undermined at a time when agriculture is facing a most difficult challenge. On the one hand the prices of the things he has to sell are going down and on the other hand the prices of the things he has to buy are rising. After all, one reason that we are here is to endeavour to bring about, through discussion, improvement in conditions when they are adverse.
The government have the information. It is another thing they keep in cold storage, along with a lot of other surpluses they have. We ask them, even at this late date, to open up that government refrigerator and reveal the situation with respect to trade, agriculture and the workers of this country.

Mr. Speaker, before this debate concludes I should like to say a few words on a matter which is of considerable importance to a great many workers in this country. It is a matter concerning which I sought to ask a question this afternoon on the orders of the day, to which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has agreed to get an answer as soon as possible. My request, as I shall develop it in a moment or two, is that that answer should be obtained and given to the house today.
Before I comment further on that subject, perhaps I might be permitted for a moment to express my regret that I had to be away from the house and away from the building at the time the vote was called on the amendment moved by the official opposition. It was only because of the sudden passing of a close personal friend that I had to leave the building and miss the vote, much to my regret. As hon. members are aware, that amendment included a plea for health insurance, which I cannot now discuss, but like my colleagues I would have voted for it gladly.
On the orders of the day this afternoon I asked the Minister of Transport if he was aware of a report in today's Winnipeg Free Press, part of which now appears as a Canadian Press dispatch in this afternoon's Ottawa Journal. I should like to give the house the main part of the story as it appears in the Free Press, for the Free Press gives the context in a way that is missing from the story that hon. members are reading at this moment on the front page of the Ottawa Journal. The Winnipeg Free Press story reads as follows:
F. H. Keefe, general manager of C.N.R. western lines, at a banquet of Beaver lodge, local 691,
The Address-Mr. Knowles brotherhood of railroad trainmen, Thursday night, said that because of dwindling traffic it had been necessary to make periodic lay-offs.
According to the Free Press report Mr. Keefe went on to say:
"We have been told", he said, "that this year we must reduce our annual maintenance budget by $5 million. And unless we can balance our budget the president has told us he is going to replace the present railway management."
Because that last paragraph is before hon. members in the evening edition of the Ottawa Journal they know the wording of that statement, but I point out that it was made in the context of a discussion by Mr. Keefe about the periodic lay-offs that have been necessary on the C.N.R. It is that aspect of it to which I ask the Minister of Transport to address himself in particular. As hon. members know, for the past year or more there has been hanging over the heads of C.N.R. employees across the country the fear of further unemployment. Hundreds of employees have been laid off in various parts of the system from coast to coast. In addition, there have been a number of instances of shops being transferred from one city to another, all of which has resulted in a terrible state of uncertainty and in serious damage to morale so far as the employees of Canadian National Railways are concerned.
This announcement that the president has told the management that they must reduce their annual maintenance budget by $5 million and balance the budget or be fired will certainly add to that uncertainty. It raises the question of whether the management will feel that in order to save their own jobs they have to lay off more employees and cut down their maintenance costs. I suggest that in view of the seriousness of the situation that arises from a statement such as this having been made by a responsible official of Canadian National Railways, the Minister of Transport should make a further statement about this matter in the house today.

I have one on the order paper about the pension position of employees who are laid off just a few years before they would qualify for their pensions. I know of cases where the employees concerned feel they have been treated quite unfairly.
It would appear from Mr. Keefe's statement that now some sort of ultimatum has been handed down by the president of the railway which has put those just below him in the position where they feel that in order to save their own jobs they have to be tough with the employees of the system generally. An announcement like that is certainly a sample of bad public relations, if nothing else; and if it is a serious announcement, if it means what it says, it represents a policy which should be reversed.
My reason for rising at this time is to make a plea that the Minister of Transport not let this matter wait until Monday, when questions might be asked on orders of the day, but that he make a statement some time today clearing up the whole situation. Let us have it clear that employee relationships on the C.N.R. are not run by a series of ultimatums from the president. Let us have the C.N.R.'s employee relationships put on a decent and proper basis, one that will be fair to all concerned, in this great national system.

Perhaps it is in Quebec. I believe it forms the boundary of the state of Maine. That would come under the jurisdiction of the international joint commission, as I shall show in a moment.
Problems associated with the use, flow and levels of international boundary waters can be resolved by reference to the international joint commission, which operates under the provisions of the boundary waters treaty of 1909. Similarly, problems associated with works in waters south of the international boundary, that cause flooding back across the boundary, are also under the jurisdiction of the international joint commission.
By article 2 of the boundary waters treaty, the government of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction and control of the use of all waters within Canada, which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary, and has the right to divert and use these waters within Canada. The United States has the same rights south of the boundary. Therefore these matters are not within the jurisdiction of the international joint commission. This international rivers bill is designed to deal with these matters, since no other legislation covers regulation in this field.
At the present time the development and utilization in Canada of waters that eventually pass beyond the boundaries and out of the control of this country is a matter of ever-increasing importance in the development of the Canadian economy. This is true of the Columbia river system and similar watersheds. The use of such waters has to be viewed not only in its present implications, and in the light of our relations with the United States, but also in the light of the future water and power requirements of Canada and of Canadians. Any short-run
International Rivers
advantage that might accrue from an immediate utilization of these resources should, of course, receive serious consideration.
However, it will be the duty of the government of Canada to make sure that the short-run advantage is consistent with long-term planning. The demand for hydroelectric power in Canada is insatiable; in fact, our industrial economy is largely built on low-cost electricity. In 1920, 5.6 billion kilowatt hours were produced. By 1928, this figure had nearly tripled to 16.3 billion. By 1941 the 1928 figure had more than doubled to 33.3 billion, and by the end of 1954 production had reached approximately 70 billion kilowatt hours. Within the year 1954 new installations both hydro and thermal generating electric power reached an all-time record -approximately 1,875,000 horsepower completed within that one year. The total installed capacity in Canada now stands at over 18 million horsepower, with another 4 million horsepower actually under construction as of January 1, 1955. Obviously it would be a shortsighted policy indeed that would jeopardize the power resources of Canada for a short-term advantage, or for an inadequate return.
We in Canada are apt to have the comfortable feeling that we still have an abundance of undeveloped hydroelectric power. However, much of our potential resources are in remote districts and do not warrant development at the present time. I think I can say that only two provinces, Quebec and British Columbia, are in the happy position of having sufficient accessible undeveloped power to meet their requirements well into the future. Ontario is now developing the power resources of the St. Lawrence river, which is their last major source of low-cost hydroelectric power. With this in mind, our duty to future generations is obvious, and that is to conserve carefully our remaining hydroelectric potential, in order to permit the further development of Canadian industries, and the further advance in the Canadian standard of living.
It is the prime purpose of this international rivers bill to ensure that the long-term national interest is safeguarded and is not prejudiced by development planned to serve immediate local purposes that may be inconsistent with the longer view. This legislation when enacted will enable the government to control, by licensing, the construction, operation and maintenance of works in Canada that affect international rivers. The purpose will be to ensure the most advantageous development of a water system, taking into account alternative development opportunities that may exist now, or that may open

International Rivers
up in the future. Control will also be exercised over projects within Canada which have as a prime objective the creation of energy or other benefits outside of Canada. It is essential that the terms under which any such projects are authorized include appropriate safeguards to protect national interests.
As I have said before, in recent years we have begun to realize that water is not a limitless resource, nor is its development purely a local problem. There is fairly general agreement that we cannot afford to waste water and that every effort must be made to use our water resources efficiently. We have to take into account, when planning the use of our water resources, the various implications for industrial, regional, national and international development.
We used to think of development in terms of a single project. It is now necessary to think in much broader terms: to consider the effects which a number of projects may have on one watershed, and still further, to consider how the development of one watershed may affect the future use of water in an adjacent basin. Diversions, especially of flood waters, from one major drainage area to another, have become possible as a result of new developments in technology, thus making possible the co-ordinated use of our various sources of energy. Where adjoining watersheds exhibit different characteristics as to storage capacity and control, there is a strong argument for their physical inter-connection. Even when inter-basin transfers of water are out of the question, it still may be possible for one of its major by-products, hydroelectric power, to provide the means for co-ordination.
Economies in long distance transmission have made it possible to move electricity to load centres at least 500 miles away, and progress continues in extending these distances. In concerning ourselves with international river developments, we therefore need perspective. We must be prepared to look beyond the basins themselves to the ramifications in terms of energy, and the facilities for its effective use, before determining the effect that a specific project may have on the Canadian economy as a whole.
This means that careful consideration will have to be given to all proposals which involve the appropriation by outside interests, for the long term, or perhaps in perpetuity, of water resources of potential value to Canada. We must first find out whether we can make effective use of these water resources within Canada. If it is in our national interest to facilitate downriver utilization of water in another country, as a result of works undertaken in Canada, then we must make sure
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur).!
that Canadians obtain benefits commensurate with the water resources thus being provided to our neighbours.
In working out appropriate arrangements with our friends to the south, we must behave as reasonable neighbours do, perhaps even acting as partners in some of these vast undertakings. We must be prepared to settle many an issue in an atmosphere of give and take. Americans and Canadians have acquired a good deal of experience in resolving certain international water problems through the operations of the international joint commission. Similarly, it should be possible to resolve any problems th.at may arise out of developments affecting international rivers in a friendly and co-operative spirit.
I do not propose to deal today with the technical and legal details of this bill. That can be done much better when this matter is dealt with in the standing committee on external affairs, to which the bill will be referred after it has received second reading. But perhaps I might deal with two questions: Are the policies which have led the government to introduce this bill in line with the principles of the boundary waters treaty, as they have evolved over the last close to half a century? Is what we are proposing similar to practice in the United States designed to ensure the effective development of their own water resources? The answer to both these questions is yes. Let me elaborate.
As I have already pointed out, article 2 of the boundary waters treaty states that each country shall have, and I quote,
. . . the exclusive jurisdiction and control over the use and diversion, whether temporary or permanent, of all waters on its own side of the line which, in their natural channels, would flow across the boundary.
Thus the treaty makes it quite explicit that Canada has complete authority over rivers flowing within her boundaries, leaving it to the government of Canada to control the use, flow, and levels of such rivers within our own territory, and to deal with any projects within Canada that might interfere with the natural flow of international rivers.
However, in exercising these rights Canada must bear in mind the rights of persons who may be affected by projects altering the natural flow of international rivers, or by the construction of storage dams and similar works which regulate the flow of waters. If such persons are injured, whether they are citizens of the United States or of Canada, they are entitled to compensation. They may come before the courts of the country that is interfering with the natural flow of international rivers, and claim compensation, whether or not they are citizens of that country.

This, we think, is a sound principle, for the rights of the individuals in both countries are thus protected. But it means that we in Canada must be very careful in granting any licenses that would create new vested interests outside our country. For, if at some future date there were promising opportunities to use Canadian water resources more effectively in our own country, vested interests in the United States might well have substantial claims on Canada.
The principle of compensation, as it has developed, covers all interests, including both private and public interests. An example of this is the case of the application for authority to build a dam on the Saint John river at Grand Falls, New Brunswick, which had the effect of raising the water levels in the international section of that river. The international joint commission granted its approval of the flooding at the boundary only after prolonged hearings, and on condition that the Canadian applicant carry out the terms of an agreement which the applicant had entered into with a United States company during the course of the hearings.
That agreement in effect conceded the validity of the arguments presented so forcibly to the international joint commission by counsel for the United States government. The counsel for the United States asserted that the "protection and indemnity" provision of the treaty did not relate exclusively to physical damage, but included also "compensation" and "a share in the benefits", which could be ordered by the international joint commission in any form desired by the United States, including the delivery of electric power. He asserted furthermore, that the compensation must take account of all interests, including the public interests of the United States and its states, as well as those of the private individuals whose property would be flooded. Finally, counsel claimed specifically on behalf of the United States a share of the power generated at the downstream site in Canada, proportional to the additional head made available by flooding in the United States and the share of the flow thus provided by the United States.
This point of view of the United States government was accepted by Canada. It is this type of thinking which the Canadian government intends to apply in administering the provisions of the international rivers bill when enacted.
Now there will be cases where the project involves the storage of water in Canada, and its release in a regulated flow. This may constitute a very valuable service to the downstream country. Not only may it reduce the damage from floods, but, through the 50433-56
International Rivers
conservation of flood waters, it may also make additional water available to the downstream country for power generation, or other purposes, during periods of low natural flow. Since the downstream country has no claim to this service, it is evident that Canada can reasonably require recompense in acceptable form if the downstream country requests us to provide the service.
Numerous formulae have been advanced to cover situations such as these. The resultant power might be divided equally, based on the thesis that, while the downstream country is providing the "head", the upstream country is providing the "flow". Head and flow together constitute power. One without the other is useless. The actual proportion of the power benefits received by the upstream and downstream countries will depend on the merits of each case; but there is little doubt that both countries will expect to get a reasonable share of the power developed as a result of joint efforts.
This important question of the great benefit conferred on downstream power plants by upstream storage is receiving increasing recognition in the proposals to govern downstream benefit settlements being worked out among the various states south of the border. The draft Columbia interstate compact, prepared by a commission which includes representatives of Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Utah, Wyoming and the United States government, in providing for the allocation of power to be generated at downstream plants recognizes the contribution which will be made by storage and regulation of flow in the upstream states.
In guarding the national interest, we must be sure that any arrangements between Canadian and American interests are concluded at arm's length; that they are bound up in long-term contracts between responsible utilities; and that the recompense in power or cash for the resultant benefits in the downstream country bears a close relationship to a fair market price of the electricity so generated, as well as to the value to Canada of alternative water resource developments solely in this country. For example, unless the cost of electricity to the beneficiaries in the United States is comparable with that of the best alternative project within their own control, we would have good reason to be sceptical. As far as Canada is concerned, in order to be acceptable in the national interest, any private arrangement would have to ensure an optimum return in perpetuity and in real terms. By real terms I mean the going price of power from time to time, or better, compensation by an appropriate block of power delivered in Canada. Unless

International Rivers
its terms fully accord with these requirements, governmental approval of the arrangement may have to be denied.
The principle that adequate compensation is a condition attached to the right of each country to exercise full control over waters flowing across the boundary was incorporated in the boundary waters treaty at the insistence of the United States secretary of state, Elihu Root. It was accepted by Canada and thus it became a fundamental principle of the treaty, having general application for the future.
The United States government has since, through the federal power commission, exercised authority over the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements in that country. As and when the international rivers bill becomes law, Canada will be exercising similar control over our international waters. This bill asserts the accepted principle that Canadians have full control over waters within Canada, and first call on their use.
In conclusion, I would like to emphasize again that the authority asked for in this bill will enable the Canadian government to ensure that development and utilization of Canadian water resources covered by this legislation will be carried out in an efficient manner, thus protecting the national interests of this and future generations.
Hon. members will have noticed that international law and international practice have had much to do with the drafting of this bill. It seems to me that hon. members should be given an opportunity to discuss the provisions of the bill in committee, where they will have the guidance of General McNaughton and other experts on the subject matter of the bill. Since external affairs are involved, the appropriate committee would seem to be the committee on external affairs. Mr. Speaker, I would ask that, after this bill receives second reading, it be referred to the committee on external affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been very much interested in the speech just made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in introducing this bill, and personally I am gratified that he has decided to have it sent to the standing committee on external affairs. When I spoke in the throne speech debate I asked that that be done, and I believe that committee can do an excellent job in considering this particular measure. In fact this is the type of bill which can best be handled by a committee of the house. Because we view the measure in this way we are not opposing second reading of the bill but we

would like to make it clear that although we agree to let it have second reading in order that it may go to a committee, we are reserving the right to make a decision as to what shall be done after the bill has been through the committee and has come back to the house.
In his remarks the minister did not explain that the bill arises largely by reason of a dispute between the government of Canada and the government of the province of British Columbia. The latter government have made an agreement with the Kaiser interests in the United States under the terms of which that firm is to erect a dam across the lower end of the Arrow lakes, these lakes being an enlargement of the Columbia river.
Apparently the provincial government believe they have made a good bargain. They are to get quite substantial payments from the company and in addition a certain percentage of the power that is produced in the United States by reason of the dam being erected in Canada. The government of Canada apparently object to this agreement, and arising out of this controversy we have the present bill. I believe that the bill is of great importance because of this controversy, and also for other reasons.
In looking at the map of Canada I find that there are several important rivers which flow from Canada into the United States and accordingly would be subject to the terms of the bill. Actually there are not as many of these rivers as one would think. First there is the Saint John fiver which apparently rises in Quebec, flows into the United States and then into New Brunswick, but the minister has said tonight that it would not be subject to the terms of the bill.

speechtext:
That is one of the questions which will have to be worked out in the committee. There seem to be no other rivers of any size which flow from Canada into the United States until we come to the Milk river in Alberta. There are two small ones in Saskatchewan, the Souris river and Frenchman river. One of the members from

Saskatchewan tells me that he has never heard of Frenchman river, so I take it that one at least is not of great importance.
But once you get to the province of British Columbia there are several great rivers which will be affected by the bill. First of all there are the rivers in the Columbia river system including not only the Columbia itself but also the Kootenay, which is a tributary of the Columbia, and the Okanagan and Similkameen, all quite important rivers. In the Columbia river system there are also three great mountain lakes, Kootenay lake, the Arrow lakes, which as I said before are really a widening of the Columbia river for well over 100 miles, and Okanagan lake. All these lakes, therefore, will be subject to the terms of this bill.
Then there are the rivers which flow out of British Columbia into the panhandle of Alaska, notably the Stikine river and the Taku river. These are very large rivers, and it is of significance that on the Taku river the Frobisher interests plan to construct a great smelter which will be operated by power derived from the headwaters of the Yukon river. As I read the bill the Taku river will be subject to its terms. The Yukon river itself also will be subject to the terms of the bill because, as hon. members know, it flows from the Yukon Territory through the territory of Alaska. That may not seem important at the moment because the dominion government controls the Yukon Territory; but if the Yukon should become a province, which I am quite sure it will eventually, then it will be in the same position as the province of British Columbia is today with regard to the Columbia river system. The bill, therefore, affects some very important rivers in western Canada.
Presumably it will affect those rivers a long way from the boundary. In other words it does not affect them only at the boundary or within a few miles of the boundary; it affects them many miles back. For example, on the main Columbia river there is a wonderful power site several hundred miles north of the boundary at a place called Mica creek, which is up near the top of the big bend of the Columbia. Eventually at that point, and I hope at an early date, a dam will be erected and a project constructed which will cost, General McNaughton told the committee on external affairs last year, about $425 million and will produce a tremendous amount of power. I do not have the exact figure at hand at the moment, but that Mica creek project will be a very large power development.
The question arises in one's mind as to whether that Mica creek dam project also 50433-56J
International Rivers
is going to be subject to the control of the dominion government under the provisions of this bill. The importance of the bill is very far-reaching, much more far-reaching than one would think at first glance. What is done on the Columbia river system will affect the people living in the interior of British Columbia for the next 100 or 200 years. This is not a short-term problem. It is vital to the development of that whole part of western Canada. This is one of the reasons I heartily agree with the minister when he says that the bill should go to the committee for study.
Another reason is that this is a brand new type of legislation. Offhand I cannot think of any similar legislation on the Canadian statute books. Parliament is dealing with a new problem, and for that reason too it is important that the bill be studied by a committee.
I believe the whole foundation of the bill is contained in the words-I cannot refer to a section, Mr. Speaker, but these words are used-"developing the water resources in the national interest". That is what this bill aims to do, develop the water resources of Canada in the national interest. Mind you, it goes further than covering future developments. The bill provides for taking licensing control over the existing developments. If there is a dam or power plant already in existence, under the terms of this bill that plant is now subject to licence. There are several large power plants on the Kootenay river just before it flows into the Columbia, and as I read the bill those plants will have to obtain licences within a year, otherwise the dominion government can demolish them. I propose to say something about this power of demolition a little later.
Another reason the bill should be considered by the committee is that it involves very grave constitutional questions. The provinces of Canada have always been very jealous of their jurisdiction over property and civil rights, and that is one reason the government of British Columbia is so concerned about this measure. General McNaughton recognized that in his statement to the external affairs committee last year. I have here the proceedings of that committee, and I am quoting from General McNaughton's evidence at page 174. He said:
So from the commission point of view, that project-
He is referring to the Mica creek project, -could be cleared for construction at any time within a year. The people to build it, the responsibility of building that dam, lies with the provincial government.
This is General McNaughton speaking.
They must say whether they are going to build it themselves through the B.C. power commission

International Rivers
or whether they are going to bring in a group of private interests to build it. All these things are very definite possibilities, but the decision will lie with the provincial government.
Then I asked him:
Q. The dominion government would take no part in the construction of these developments?
A. The federal government of Canada has the over-all responsibility of negotiations with the United States.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed that out tonight.
It is very essential that the negotiations in regard to the benefits that come from the regulated water and controlled flow, and so on, should be settled and will have to be settled before it would be wise for the provincial government to authorize someone to go ahead and build it.
General McNaughton's own evidence shows quite clearly that the provincial government is vitally interested in the Mica creek project, as well as any other projects on the Columbia river system.
Another reason the bill requires careful study was dealt with by the minister this evening when he mentioned downstream benefits. This doctrine of downstream benefits has only been worked out lately. General McNaughton told us that Canada was only able to make headway on that argument because the northwest states got into an argument between the upstream and downstream states, with the upstream states insisting that they should get benefits from the downstream states. Having established that principle in the fighting between themselves, Canada was able to come along and take advantage of their argument.
General McNaughton dealt with this question too, and at page 166 of the committee evidence he said:
As I mentioned before, power is the product of head and flow, the factors come in equally on it and it does seem and has seemed to those of us who are studying the matter, and a lot of other people as well, that when this additional power which is derived without any cost in the generating plant, because generating plants are idle unless the required flow is provided to them, that power which is produced in that way should be divided between the two countries. That has been the very forceful contention made to us by the government of British Columbia and it is the crux of the discussion which is going on with the United States.
The external affairs committee members were very much impressed by General McNaughton's evidence about downstream benefits, and in their report they inserted this paragraph:
Your committee also approves of the stand taken by the Canadian section of the international joint commission concerning recompense for downstream benefits on the Columbia river system.
Before I go on to deal with the Columbia system itself in some detail I should like to refer to the powers taken in this bill to seize works which have not been properly licensed.

As I say, they can be seized by the dominion government and can be removed, destroyed or otherwise disposed of. Now, it looks as though the province of British Columbia, if it cannot have the Kaiser people build a dam, may try to go ahead and build a dam itself with government funds. Under the seizure powers we can get into a position, Mr. Speaker, where the British Columbia government, having built a dam without getting a licence from the dominion government, may then have that dam removed by the dominion government.
Talk about Formosa. I can picture to myself Premier Bennett standing on this dam, and in the front line trenches will be the little corporal from Macleod with all the other Social Crediters who have come from the province of Alberta into British Columbia. Premier Bennett will have around him all the rest of his supporters who are not quite sure what Social Credit is, but anyway there they are.
